title: Three Reasons You Shouldn't Use Your Browser's Password Manager (and What to Use Instead)
body:
Built-in tools have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 4, 2026
            
            
                        Credit:  Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    
        
        Most modern browsers have built-in password management, allowing you to save your credentials and automatically fill them when logging into your accounts on various websites. And while Google Password Manager on Chrome and similar tools in other browsers like Firefox, Brave, and Microsoft Edge certainly simplify the process of storing and using stronger passwords, they have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality. Here's why you should use a dedicated password manager instead.Browser password managers only work within the browserIf you store your passwords in your browser, it can fill your credentials on websites within the browser itself. (If you're an Android user, Google Password Manager also syncs to your device and works across any browser or app.) But if you use multiple browsers or want to log into apps on your iPhone or PC, you'll have to manually copy and paste your password from the browser into those form fields—not ideal, from a standpoint of both convenience and security. Browser password managers are more vulnerable to security risksBrowser password management is, on a basic level, secure: Google uses the same AES encryption in transit and at rest that many dedicated password managers do, and allows it you to add biometric authentication for auto-filling credentials. However, they're not zero-knowledge by default: Google manages your encryption key unless you enable on-device encryption so that your vault can only be unlocked on your device, by you, with your Google password or biometrics. Firefox also uses AES-256 encryption and has a "primary password" feature to protect your stored data, without which anyone who has access to your computer or browser profile can view your saved passwords. It's on the user to add these layers of security, as they're not on by default.As Wired points out, the more serious problem isn't encryption, but rather the risk inherent in storing passwords in a high-value account that could be targeted—either by someone who gains access to your device or as part of a takeover attempt, such as a phishing or credential stuffing attack. This creates a single point of failure, and if someone gets into your Google account or your browser of choice, your passwords for everything else are also compromised. Browser password managers have only basic featuresBrowser password managers do basically one thing, which is store your login credentials and fill them in on websites when you visit them in the browser. Google Password Manager will also alert you if your password has been compromised in a breach, but most browsers lack any additional tools and features, such as password customization, secure sharing, email masking, emergency access, and storage for payment cards, identity data, and documents. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Use a dedicated third-party password manager insteadThe solution is to opt for a dedicated password manager that works across platforms and devices and offers a layer of protection outside of your browser. There are many excellent password managers to choose from, including free services like Bitwarden and privacy-focused Proton Pass (which also has a decent free tier). The best password managers also have features like secure file storage, encrypted credential sharing, and data breach monitoring, making them useful tools in your privacy and security arsenal. Of course, even a browser password manager is better than nothing at all, if the alternative is to reuse the same easy-to-remember credentials across your accounts. (It's also likely your reused passwords don't meet basic security standards and can be easily guessed.) Password storage in Chrome, Firefox, and other browsers do reduce the friction of shifting to strong, unique passwords for your accounts, and that alone is a solid step. But a third-party password manager is a superior choice if you're willing to invest a bit of time and energy into setting it up. 
            
                        
                
                    
                                            
                
                
                                            
    More by Emily

title: Firefox Can Now Block Ads on iOS (but You Have to Enable It)
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

        September 1, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Kenneth Cheung / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device, as Mozilla is officially rolling out native ad blocking.
                                            Most ads will be blocked, but users will still see search engine ads and sponsored content from Firefox.
                                            The feature is off by default, so you need to enable it yourself if you want to use it.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device. Following a slow "experimental" period, Mozilla is now officially rolling out native ad blocking, which you can enable once the tool is available in your app. According to Mozilla's support page detailing the new feature, Firefox's new feature can block third-party ad networks and exchanges along with many third-party ads served on websites at the network level. It can also block ad-related trackers, pop-ups, and overlays. The platform is still letting some ads through, though: For example, you'll still see ads in search results from engines like Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo, as well as sponsored content on the Firefox Home and New Tab pages. There may also be ads that aren't covered by the EasyList filter list. Of course, Firefox isn't the only browser to natively block ads on iOS. For example, both DuckDuckGo and Brave have built-in ad blocking in their mobile apps and also allow you to disable their own search ads. Note that ad-blocking functionality doesn't extend outside of the Firefox iOS app, but URL filters in iOS 26, along with a third-party app like Wipr 2, can block ads in other apps. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Ad blocking in Firefox will be off by default. To enable it, open the iOS app, tap the three dots, and go to Settings > Browsing. Under the Content header, toggle on Ad Blocker. You can do this from the Site menu by tapping Ad Blocker (underneath the site name and URL), which will open the Browsing menu directly. The site menu will show you at a glance whether ad blocking is on or off.

            Credit: Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft Outlook is down for many users as of Monday afternoon.
                                            Downdetector highlights tens of thousands of users reports suggesting issues with Outlook.
                                            In addition, other Microsoft services, including Microsoft 365, are also down.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're trying to check your inbox or send an email in Microsoft Outlook, only to find the app uncooperative, you're not alone. Outlook is currently down for many users as of Monday afternoon. That's apparent to anyone who can't get the app to work: Downdetector, which highlights user reports for app outages, shows tens of thousands of reports as of 3:00 p.m. ET, and while the rate of reports does seem to be decreasing, thousands of reports keep coming in with every refresh.  As CNET reports, Microsoft has officially confirmed the outage itself. The company posted on its Microsoft 365 Status X account, stating: “We’ve identified an issue with an authentication component which is contributing to impact. To address this, we’ve developed a remediation strategy, and we’re applying it to a portion of infrastructure to test its efficacy. Once we’ve confirmed this resolves impact, we’ll apply the solution more broadly. For more information, please see EX1464935 in the admin center.”As such, the company should be rolling out a fix in due time, though it's difficult to say how long that may be. Recent outages have been fixed in a matter of hours, while others have stretched into the following day. At the time of writing, Downdetector shows that 38% of users are reporting issues receiving messages in Outlook, while 24% report issues with the app, and 21% with logging in. 
As it happens, Outlook isn't the only Microsoft product facing issues: Users report that Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Store, Microsoft Azur  and Microsoft 365 in general are experiencing  issues. In addition, OpenAI users are reporting issues with ChatGPT. 
            
                What do you think so far?

                Key Takeaways
                                            ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok are all experiencing downtime Thursday morning.
                                            OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX AI all confirm issues with their platforms.
                                            It's not clear what the root cause of the issue is at this time, or whether the outages are related.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you had trouble accessing AI platforms Thursday morning, you're not alone. Apps and services, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok, were down, or experienced issues with service. ChatGPT and Grok were both unresponsive when I tried to use them, while Claude appeared to respond, at least for me. ChatGPT appears to be experiencing the most issues, at least per Downdetector. The site, which accepts user reports of issues with apps and services, currently shows tens of thousands of reports for ChatGPT alone. Claude and Grok had fewer reports, but still many (thousands) over the course of this morning. According to OpenAI's status page, the company had experienced issues with both ChatGPT and Codex. Anthropic had also acknowledged issues with Claude, including for its Mythos 5.1, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5 models, and said it is working on a fix. SpaceXAI shows that all Grok functions appear to be down at this time. As of 1:19 p.m. ET, all three services now report that they're now up and running. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's not clear exactly what caused these issues, or if they were all related to one another. Typically, outages like these are solved relatively quickly, so it's not a surprise that all three were able to get their systems back by early afternoon. I'll continue to monitor the situation and update this piece accordingly.

title: TikTok Just Announced These Four New Features for Comments
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            TikTok announced four new features coming to its comment section over the next month.
                                            Next month, the app will roll out voice comments, which will let users record and post audio up to 60 seconds.
                                            Creators can add polls to their comment sections to invite viewers to vote on up to five options at a time.
                                            Finally, TikTok is rolling out photo carousel and Live Photos comments as well.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        TikTok is famous for its addictive algorithm. And while the videos are certainly the app's main focus, I find the most entertainment in the comments. TikTok commenters can be hilarious, especially since they can use both text and photos to make their jokes. Social media comments are often vile, and while TikTok isn't immune to trolls and their ilk, its comments are generally something else. Now, the comments are changing. On Thursday, TikTok announced four new features that will make comments more visual, interactive, and, well, loud. Not all of these features are out quite yet, but by next month, you might not recognize TikTok's comment section. Text and photo comments aren't going anywhere, but you may find that the comment section is about to get a bit louder. Starting next month, TikTok will support voice comments up to 60 seconds long, which adds a wholly unique type of comment to the mix. Based on TikTok's press release, you can still attach a text-based comment to your voice comment, similar to how photo comments work.While friends may post voice comments on each other's videos à la voice memos in a group chat, I'm guessing that commenters in general will use this feature in ways TikTok doesn't necessarily intend. In fact, this may birth a new type of meme, where users spam videos with obnoxious sound effects and reaction sounds. Think the sounds added to meme edits of viral videos, but in comment form. It's going to be messy, and, likely, hysterical.   
Starting this week, you may see a new interactive element to TikTok comments: polls. TikTok says creators can add polls to the comments of their videos, with up to five voting options per poll. Rather than ask for opinions in the comments, creators can use a poll instead. Creators can choose how long voting lasts, and watch votes appear in real time. It's a small change, but one that could be useful to both big and small creators looking for input from their viewers. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
You're no longer limited to posting static images in TikTok's comments. TikTok now supports uploading Live Photos to comments, which should also prove interesting. I could see people thinking they're posting a standard image, but accidentally uploading a Live Photo instead. But seeing as users already know how to add GIFs to comments, I'm not sure how many will want to upload Live Photos. This one might be reserved more for friends commenting on friends' videos, but we'll have to see how users react to know for sure. This last update is perhaps a bit more useful than Live Photo comments. TikTok says it's working on allowing users to upload up to nine photos in one comment, which means the comments section may be literally full of pictures once this launches en masse.  Like standard carousels, users will be able to swipe through your photo uploads, including in a full-screen view. This one will roll out over the course of this month.

title: These Google Maps and Apple Maps Alternatives Still Call It ‘Lake Ontario’ (for Now)
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 2, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Following Trump's executive order, Google Maps and Apple Maps have renamed Lake Ontario "Lake America."
                                            Google says it follows the U.S. Geographic Names Information System, and has updated its map accordingly.
                                            Trump directly appealed to Apple, on the other hand, to change the name on its map.
                                            Some other navigation apps have not changed Lake Ontario's name—at least, not yet.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America." The move was retaliation against Canada for walking away from contentious trade talks and in spite of the fact that Lake Ontario's name has nothing to do with the Canadian province. Regardless, tech companies are now dealing with the consequences.Why did Google Maps change Lake Ontario's name?If you live in the U.S., you may have opened Google Maps this past weekend to see that the app had already changed Lake Ontario's name. Even if you don't live in the U.S., you may see the name change: As it happens, there are now three different naming schemes for the lake in Google's navigation app. If you use the app in the U.S., you'll see "Lake America." If you use it in Canada, you'll see "Lake Ontario." If you use it anywhere else in the world, you'll see "Lake Ontario (Lake America)." Thanks, Google.
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Google
                    
    
Google did the same when Trump "changed" the name of the Gulf of Mexico to "Gulf of America." While Google explains in a blog post that its policy is to follow the naming conventions of the U.S. Geographic Names Information System, it's also arguable that the company doesn't want to get into hot water with the Trump Administration, lest it be punished with future policies that could hurt its trillion-dollar business. Now, Apple Maps is in the same boat. While Apple's app kept "Lake Ontario" on its map longer than Google, it has since changed the name as well. Trump reportedly urged Apple directly to make the switch. (Like Google, the company previously changed the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America as well.) 
Whether you consider it basic bureaucratic compliance or corporate cowardice, Google Maps and Apple Maps now call the lake by its "new" name. It doesn't affect how the apps work (maybe unless you're looking for directions to, or information about, Lake Ontario), but if the change rankles you, you have other options: As it stands, there are now two key alternatives that still label it "Lake Ontario."As of this writing, only a couple of apps available to download call Lake Ontario by its official/"former" name. Whether that will remain true as the week goes on remains a question, but for now, the following apps are still reflecting the global consensus:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
MapQuestOrganic MapsTechnically, Waze also still calls it Lake Ontario on its map, and the name pops up when you start to search for it. But once you tap the result, the app then swaps the name to Lake America. That's to be expected, given Google owns Waze, but the app initially tricked me into thinking it had maintained the previous status quo.Will other apps change Lake Ontario's name?Will these apps maintain the Lake Ontario name over the long term? When I first published this article, Apple hadn't changed the name, but I had expected them to. As I said above, Apple ultimately changed the Gulf of Mexico's name, so it followed that it would likely do the same with the lake. However, MapQuest and Organic Maps still call the Gulf of Mexico by its correct name, so chances are good they'll keep Lake Ontario on their maps for the foreseeable future.

title: We Now Know When Apple's Big iPhone Event Will Happen
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        August 26, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Viva Tung/Lifehacker
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple just announced a new keynote, where the company is expected to announce the latest iPhones.
                                            Leaks and rumors suggest Apple will reveal the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which should offer small upgrades over the iPhone 17 Pro.
                                            The star of the show will be the iPhone Ultra, Apple's first foldable iPhone (and likely the company's most expensive iPhone to date).
                                            The keynote starts at 10 a.m. PT on Wednesday, Sept. 9.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        You don't need to follow leaks and rumors to know that Apple will announce the iPhone 18 next month. The company has revealed new iPhones once a year every year since its first smartphone launch back in 2007. The real unknown, of course, is what day exactly Apple will make these announcements. As of Wednesday, we know for sure. Ahead of the event, make sure to enter Lifehacker's Big Guessing Game. The quiz is now in its third round, and each correct guess gets you the chance to win the latest Apple Watch.Apple just announced its next big iPhone eventApple has set an official time and date for its iPhone 18 announcement. The company is scheduled to kick off its keynote on Wednesday, Sept. 9 at 10 a.m. PT. While Apple is inviting some media members to attend in person, anyone can watch the presentation live online. Apple's senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, Greg Joswiak, confirmed the keynote in a post on X:

    
        This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.
    

What will Apple announce at its iPhone event?We don't know for sure what Apple will reveal on Sept. 9, but leaks and rumors give us some good guesses. The math tells us that Apple will go from the iPhone 17 to the iPhone 18 this year, while the leaks suggest that we'll see the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the foldable "iPhone Ultra."(Apple may delay the standard iPhone 18 to 2027, per rumors.) 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max will likely be standard upgrades from the iPhone 17 Pro series: Expect better cameras, bigger batteries, new colors (including the new "light blue" and "dark cherry"), the new A20 chip, and higher price tags. The star of the show will be Apple's first foldable iPhone, which will come with many of the same internals as the iPhone 18 Pros, but may ship with Touch ID instead of Face ID, and, of course, with two display types: a smaller outer display, which opens up to reveal a larger inner display. This might be Apple's most expensive iPhone yet, fetching over $2,000, but we'll have to wait and see once Apple officially announces its price tag.

title: 10 Hacks Every Proton Mail User Should Know
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Zain bin Awais/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Proton Mail is a privacy-focused mail service that strips trackers from messages, maintains zero-access encryption (meaning Proton can't read or hand over the content of your emails), and offers end-to-end encryption between Proton mailboxes. If you're a Proton user, there are a handful of other hacks you should know to maximize these privacy features and make sending and receiving emails as seamless as possible. Proton Mail is free to use if you have just one email address, but storage is limited to just 500 MB, which will fill up fast if you are receiving messages with large attachments. You can upgrade to a Plus subscription for $4 per month to get 15 GB of storage—the same amount available to most Google users—but if you don't want to pay anything, you can at least double your limit to 1 GB by completing Proton's onboarding process within 18 days of signing up. Look for a Get more storage option on the left sidebar of your mailbox, and click an action to complete the task. Once you've finished the checklist, you'll unlock an additional 500 MB of storage on your account. Reserve an email address for your child in their nameIf you have a relatively common name, it's likely that many email addresses using simple conventions, such as firstname.lastname, have already been claimed. By the time your kids are old enough to set up their own accounts, pickings may be even slimmer. You can go ahead and reserve a username through Proton Mail for them, and they have 15 years to activate it. Once they're old enough, they'll already have a private email set up. Choose an address and pay $1 toward the Proton Foundation, then save the voucher to share with your child down the line. 
Use Easy Switch to migrate external email addressesIf you're moving to Proton Mail from a different email provider or simply want all of your messages in one inbox, you can use Proton's Easy Switch feature to connect with and import from Gmail, Yahoo Mail, Outlook, and any other provider that allows IMAP access. Once Easy Switch is on, you'll be able to receive and send messages from your external address within Proton, and any mail sent to another Proton user from that address will be end-to-end encrypted. You'll retain copies of messages in your external inbox, so you don't need to make the full transition immediately. Easy Switch can also migrate your contacts and calendars. Go to Settings > Import via Easy Switch, choose your email service, and follow the prompts. Customize the Undo Send timer to recall emailsWe've all sent emails we wish we could take back thanks to a typo we didn't notice, an attachment we forgot to add, or a message we regret. Proton Mail has a delayed send feature that gives you up to 20 seconds to change your mind before your email is out of your hands. The timer is set at 10 seconds by default, but you can adjust it down to 0 or 5 seconds or up to 20. Go to Settings > Messages and composing, scroll down to the Composing section, and choose your desired time from the Undo send dropdown.Create aliases to filter mail to specific foldersThere are plenty of good reasons to use an email alias, from keeping your primary address private to easily filtering messages from mailing lists. Proton Mail supports unlimited plus addressing, meaning you can simply add a plus symbol and word after your username to create a new email—such as [username][email protected]—and receive messages in your regular inbox (with filters if you set them up). This can be done when you sign up for an account or add your email to a list. Alternatively, you can create a randomly generated email alias, which keeps your username hidden. Free users get up to 10, while paid subscribers can create unlimited aliases. On the web interface, click the security shield icon, go to Hide-my-email aliases, and click New alias. Add a password to encrypt emails to non-Proton usersMessages between Proton users are automatically encrypted end to end, but if your recipient doesn't use Proton Mail, you can set up a password for your emails to keep them private. Replies to password-protected emails are also encrypted (though your reply to that reply will require you to re-enable encryption). When you compose your message, click the padlock icon in the bottom toolbar and enter a password and password hint. You can set an expiration date as well. Note that you'll need to share the password with the recipient separately.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Set expiration timers to automatically delete emails from recipients’ inboxesAnother Proton Mail security feature is the expiration timer, which will auto-delete emails you send and receive after a set period, preventing messages from hanging around in inboxes and sent folders indefinitely. Messages that you send to other Proton Mail users as well as password-protected emails to those outside of Proton can be set to expire. If you have a paid account, you can also set emails you receive to self-destruct (in addition to auto-delete for messages in trash). Click the hourglass icon at the bottom of the message and set the expiration date and time. If you are sending a password-protected email to a non-Proton user, check the box. Then hit Set. When you take a photo, image metadata may reveal locations, times and dates, and other information that can be used to track you if it falls into the wrong hands. Proton Mail can strip that out for sent images, so you can share photos via email without giving any unnecessary data away. When you attach an image to an email draft, choose Remove metadata when prompted. Turn on Message Content Search to build a local and searchable index of your emails Because of Proton's encryption, the standard search feature reads only names, dates, email addresses, and subject lines. If you want to include message content, you'll need to enable the feature that builds a local index in your browser, protecting it from intrusion unless someone has physical access to your device. Click the search bar at the top of your inbox on the web app and tap Enable next to Search message content. Click Enable to confirm. Note that indexing does require storage space, but once complete, it'll automatically update as long as your browser is open. Activate your short domain to get a shorter, simpler addressBy default, Proton Mail addresses end in @proton.me (unless you connect your own domain). But users on paid plans have the option to add a short domain, which is simply [username]@pm.me. You can send messages from either, and both route to your inbox. The shorter address is easier to remember and share, such as when you're giving our your email over the phone. To enable it, go to Settings > Identity and addresses. You must be a paid subscriber to activate a short domain address—if you downgrade to the free plan, you will still be able to receive (but not send) messages sent to your @pm.me address.

Garmin's newest models aren't on sale, unfortunately, but this is a great time to snag slightly older models at a discount. Here are the ones I'd consider if I were buying a new Garmin today.
Garmin's Venu 3 is on sale for an all-time-low price, currently $291.90 for the larger 45-millimeter version in black. This is a full-featured fitness watch, with morning reports, ECG readings, and a 14-day battery life. It originally retailed for $449.99, and usually doesn't go below about $350 on sale days. Other Labor Day fitness watch deals: The Vivoactive 5 is on sale for $181.97 this weekend, nearly an all-time low according to price-tracking tools. It was $299.99 when it first came out, and normally sits around $229.99 now that it's not the newest model. I've long thought the Vivoactive 5 is one of Garmin's most underrated watches. It's got a sleek, lightweight style, with a touchscreen that makes it easy to use, but it still has physical buttons to start and stop your workouts. I found its heart rate and location accuracy to be very good.The best deals on Garmin Forerunners for Labor Day
Garmin's Forerunner line is the one targeted specifically at runners, but it's great for fitness of all types. The Forerunner 965, originally released in 2023, was a top-of-the-line model that is still an excellent pick. It has maps, and a ton of running analytics that you can pore over after your workouts. It's on sale right now for $499.99, normally $599.99.Other Labor Day Garmin Forerunner deals: The entry-level Forerunner 165, $199.99 (normally $249.99)The Forerunner 265, $349.99 (normally $449.99), one of my favorite running watches of all time.The Forerunner 265S, $349.99 (normally $449.99). This is the same watch as the 265, but in a smaller size and with a slightly better battery life. Labor Day Deals FAQsWhen do Labor Day sales start?Labor Day sales have already started and run through Monday, Sept. 7.
